title: Environmental DNA metabarcoding in ecological status assessment: Agreement and bias relative to traditional fish‐based evaluations
content:
eDNA metabarcoding offers a transformative opportunity for biodiversity monitoring and for tracking gradients in ecological condition, but it cannot yet be directly applied within fish-based ecological status assessment frameworks. To avoid underestimating ecological degradation in regulatory decision-making, the practical application of eDNA must explicitly incorporate the spatial extent and transport of eDNA signals and support the calibration and development of eDNA-specific metrics and indices, rather than simply transferring or replacing existing assessment methods.


Abstract

Freshwater ecosystems are experiencing unprecedented degradation worldwide. Regulatory frameworks such as the Water Framework Directive mandate standardized biological monitoring to assess ecological status against legally binding thresholds and guide restoration action. Although environmental DNA metabarcoding offers an efficient, non-invasive monitoring tool, whether water-sample eDNA can deliver reliable fish-based ecological status assessment, especially for WFD threshold decisions, remains insufficiently validated. We conducted eDNA metabarcoding and electrofishing surveys at 50 wadeable stream sites spanning four hydro-geomorphological river types in the Balaton catchment, Hungary. We calculated the Ecological Quality Ratio and Ecological Quality Class using a WFD-compliant multimetric index, quantified consistency between methods and identified the metrics driving between-method differences in assessment outcomes. Results demonstrated significant concordance between the two methods in relative site ranking of EQR values and fish assemblage structure, indicating that eDNA can capture spatial gradients of ecological degradation. However, agreement in absolute EQR values and EQC classifications was low, with eDNA generally yielding higher ecological status than electrofishing. Discrepancies were largely attributable to higher species detection by eDNA, arising mainly from the combined effects of limited detectability of rare taxa in standardized electrofishing surveys and the greater sensitivity and downstream transport of eDNA. These contrasts propagated mainly through richness-dependent metrics, ultimately resulting in divergent index scores and ecological status classifications across methods. However, the magnitude and direction of these biases varied among river types and sites. Synthesis and applications. eDNA metabarcoding offers a transformative opportunity for biodiversity monitoring and for tracking gradients in ecological condition, but it cannot yet be directly applied within fish-based ecological status assessment frameworks. To avoid underestimating ecological degradation in regulatory decision-making, the practical application of eDNA must explicitly incorporate the spatial extent and transport of eDNA signals and support the calibration and development of eDNA-specific metrics and indices, rather than simply transferring or replacing existing assessment methods.
